evals.prompt: Run the measure loop. Regional sales leads want a dashboard to decide each Monday where to send the two floating account managers. They asked for: weekly revenue by region, revenue all time, website sessions, active customers, average deal size by region, and a map. Revenue's query is in revenue.sql (Postgres; one row per region per week; customers.customer_id is unique and an order has many order_items). Nobody has written down what 'active customer' means; sales counts anyone with an open opportunity, finance counts anyone invoiced in 90 days.
assertions: Runs dashboard-spec first and writes the decision statement before reviewing any SQL
Cuts all-time revenue, website sessions and the map with reasons
Marks active customers as undefined and does not choose between the sales and finance definitions
Reviews revenue.sql and flags the order_items join as multiplying revenue
Reports G9 as NOT READY and returns to spec with the corrected query as the metric's source
Lists verification queries that show how much the revenue number changes
Stops at G9.1 asking the metric owners to confirm; does not confirm a definition itself

evals.prompt: Continuing the measure loop. The revenue owner, finance, says the corrected query is right but revenue must be booked in New York time and exclude refunded orders. The query uses UTC and doesn't look at refunds.
assertions: Treats this as G9.1 REVISE and returns to spec with finance's definition
Updates the revenue metric's definition in the spec to New York time and excluding refunded orders
Reviews the changed query again at G9 before returning to sign-off
Counts the return under the cap of 3

evals.prompt: we need a dashboard for the Monday win-back meeting. Anouk's request is in request.md, the queries we use now are in sql/ and the schema's in schema.md. Can you make sure these numbers are right before Sana's team builds it? Postgres.
assertions: Runs the stages in order: the dashboard spec first, then the SQL review, then a sign-off request to the metric owners. Fixes from the review go back into the metric definitions in the spec

The spec says which decision the dashboard serves (which plan cohorts get this week's win-back offer), gives one chart for each of Anouk's four questions in her order, and leaves page views and app downloads off, saying why
Catches that net_revenue_by_plan.sql inflates revenue: joining order_items repeats each order total once per line item, and the refunds join repeats it again for orders with more than one refund
Catches that NOT IN (SELECT subscriber_id FROM subs.test_accounts) returns no rows because test_accounts.subscriber_id can be NULL. Gives a NOT EXISTS (or equivalent) fix
Catches the integer division in weekly_churn_rate.sql (cancelled / active_start), which rounds churn down to 0 for nearly every week. Gives corrected SQL
Flags that date_trunc('week', ...) on UTC timestamps does not match the Monday-to-Sunday UK-time week Anouk asked for, and gives a fix that sets the time zone to Europe/London
Asks the named owners to sign off each metric definition (Anouk for churn and active subscribers, Callum Reyes for net revenue) and does not record any definition as signed off
Does not invent figures, targets, alert thresholds or metric owners that are not in the request

evals.prompt: The exec dashboard gets built next week and it's got one 'Active customers' tile. Finance says 41,200 for October and Growth says 58,900, and the thread in thread.md is getting heated. Both queries are in sql/, schema notes in schema.md. Just pick whichever one is right and write the spec so BI can start Monday please.
assertions: Runs the spec and the SQL review, then stops at sign-off. It does not hand BI a finished spec with the Active customers definition marked as agreed
Separates the difference in definition (Finance counts customers with a successful payment in October; Growth counts non-trial customers with a login) from the defects in the SQL
Catches that growth_active_customers.sql uses COUNT(*) over the users join, so it counts staff seats rather than customers, and gives a COUNT(DISTINCT c.customer_id) fix
Catches that last_login_at is overwritten on every login, so a customer whose users logged in during October and again since is dropped. Points to app.login_events instead
Catches that last_login_at < '2026-10-31' leaves out 31 October

Does not settle the definition on its own authority. It may recommend one, but presents the choice for a named person to sign off, and points out that the thread names no metric owner and that 'happy for analytics to call it' is not a sign-off
Reports that the sign-off gate has not passed, so the Active customers tile is not ready to build, and says who needs to decide what
Does not invent a metric owner, a reconciled Active customers figure, or a split of the 17,700 gap by cause, none of which are in the input

evals.prompt: We need a dashboard for the operations board so they can decide each month where the second van goes. The request is in request.md, the schema in schema.md, and the two queries we use today are households_served.sql and stockout_rate.sql. Make sure the numbers are right before the BI developer builds it.
assertions: Opens with the dashboard in plain words: the decision it serves (which district the second van visits next month) and the questions it answers
Gives one chart per question, each backed by a metric defined precisely enough to build (what is counted, the grain, the time window and how NULL travel_km is handled)

Catches that households_served.sql counts parcel items, not households, because the join to parcel_items repeats each visit about 14 times, and that a household visiting weekly is counted once per visit; gives corrected SQL using a distinct count of households
Catches that stockout_rate.sql divides an integer by an integer, so the rate comes out as 0 (or 100) rather than a real share, and gives corrected SQL
Says in plain words which way each bug would have moved the figure the board saw, for example demand hugely overstated
Leaves the 'total parcels ever given' counter off the dashboard, or questions it, because it does not help decide where the van goes
Names Hollis Fenwick and Esme Tarrant as the owners of their metrics and leaves each definition waiting for its owner's sign-off rather than calling it approved
Does not invent metrics, targets or data sources not in the input, such as a deprivation index or a demand forecast

evals.prompt: I'm Noor, the analyst at Pellwick Outdoor. Sales and Finance have argued about net revenue for weeks and have now handed the definition to me (handoff-thread.md). Give me the spec for the board's revenue dashboard. Their two queries are sales_net_revenue.sql and finance_net_revenue.sql, and the schema is in schema.md.
assertions: Opens with the net revenue definition it settled on, in plain words: what is included and excluded (VAT, shipping, refunds) and when revenue counts
Records the hand-off as the basis for the definition, naming Dana Ruskin and Callum Brightwater as having given the decision to Noor, and does not send the choice back to them
Settles Dana's open question on shipping charges one way or the other and says so, rather than leaving it undefined
Explains what changes for each team compared with its current query, as the thread asks
Catches that sales_net_revenue.sql sums order_total after joining order_lines, so each order is counted once per line (about three times)

Catches that `r.reason <> 'test'` in finance_net_revenue.sql also drops refunds whose reason is NULL, which is most of them, so refunds are under-deducted and net revenue is overstated; gives corrected SQL
Handles the month boundary in Europe/London rather than UTC in the SQL for the chosen definition, or flags it as needing a fix
Does not invent revenue figures, the size of the gap between the two queries, or accounting policies not in the input
